content: Buffered Penicillin G Potassium for Injection, USP can be administered either intravenously or intramuscularly. The following are detailed instructions for its use: Pediatric Patients This medication should not be administered to pediatric patients who require less than one million units per dose. Refer to the PRECAUTIONS – Pediatric Use section for further guidance. Renal Impairment Penicillin G is generally considered nontoxic, but dosage adjustments are necessary in cases of severe renal impairment. The recommended dosage regimens are as follows: For patients with a creatinine clearance of less than 10 mL/min/1.73m²: Administer a full loading dose (refer to the recommended dosages in the tables provided) followed by half of the loading dose every 8 to 10 hours. For uremic patients with a creatinine clearance greater than 10 mL/min/1.73m²: Administer a full loading dose (refer to the recommended dosages in the tables provided) followed by half of the loading dose every 4 to 5 hours. Additional dosage modifications may be required for patients with both hepatic disease and renal impairment. For most acute infections, treatment should continue for at least 48 to 72 hours after the patient becomes asymptomatic. In the case of Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections, antibiotic therapy should be maintained for a minimum of 10 days to reduce the risk of rheumatic fever. Prior to administration, parenteral drug products should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration, provided the solution and container allow for such inspection. Preparation of Solution To prepare solutions of penicillin: 1. Loosen the powder in the vial. 2. Hold the vial horizontally and rotate it while slowly directing the stream of diluent against the wall of the vial. 3. Shake the vial vigorously after adding all the diluent. Depending on the intended route of administration, use either Sterile Water for Injection, USP, or Sterile Isotonic Sodium Chloride Solution for Parenteral Use. Note that penicillins are rapidly inactivated in the presence of carbohydrate solutions at an alkaline pH. Reconstitution The amount of solvent required to achieve various concentrations of penicillin is provided in the accompanying table. If the required volume of solvent exceeds the vial's capacity, dissolve the penicillin by injecting only a portion of the solvent into the vial. Then, withdraw the resultant solution and combine it with the remaining solvent in a larger sterile container. Penicillin G Potassium for Injection, USP is highly water-soluble and can be dissolved in small amounts of Water for Injection or Sterile Isotonic Sodium Chloride Solution for Parenteral Use. All prepared solutions should be stored in a refrigerator. When refrigerated, penicillin solutions remain stable for up to seven days without significant loss of potency. Buffered Penicillin G Potassium for Injection can be administered intramuscularly or via continuous intravenous drip for dosages of 500,000, 1,000,000, or 5,000,000 units. It is also suitable for intrapleural, intraarticular, and other local installations. However, the 20,000,000-unit (20 million unit) dosage must be administered exclusively by intravenous infusion. 1. Intramuscular Injection: Keep the total injection volume small. The intramuscular route is the preferred method of administration. Solutions containing up to 100,000 units of penicillin per mL of diluent can be used with minimal discomfort. Higher concentrations of penicillin G per mL are physically possible and may be used if required by the therapy. For large doses, it may be advisable to administer aqueous solutions of penicillin via continuous intravenous drip. 2. Continuous Intravenous Drip: Determine the required volume of fluid and the rate of administration for the patient over a 24-hour period, as is standard for fluid therapy. Add the appropriate daily dosage of penicillin to this fluid. For example, if an adult patient requires 2 liters of fluid in 24 hours and a daily dosage of 10 million units of penicillin, add 5 million units to 1 liter of fluid and adjust the flow rate so that the liter is infused over 12 hours. 3. Intrapleural or Other Local Infusion: If fluid is aspirated, administer the infusion in a volume equal to one-quarter or one-half of the aspirated fluid volume. Otherwise, prepare the solution as you would for an intramuscular injection. 4. Intrathecal Use: The intrathecal administration of penicillin for meningitis must be highly individualized. This route should only be used with full consideration of the potential irritating effects of penicillin. The preferred treatment route for bacterial meningitis is intravenous administration, supplemented by intramuscular injections.
